title: John Paul Scott — the man who swam from Alcatraz to the Golden Gate
sources: Wikipedia: Alcatraz Federal Penitentiary — in its 29 years the prison claimed no prisoner ever successfully escaped; 36 prisoners made 14 attempts: 23 were caught, 6 shot dead, 2 drowned and 5 listed as 'missing and presumed drowned'; Theodore Cole and Ralph Roe vanished into a stormy bay in December 1937; the prison closed on 21 March 1963 after the June 1962 escape.

Wikipedia: June 1962 Alcatraz escape — on 16 December 1962 inmate John Paul Scott made inflatable armbands from rubber gloves and swam about 2.7 nautical miles (5 km) from Alcatraz to Fort Point, at the southern end of the Golden Gate Bridge; teenagers found him there with hypothermia and exhaustion; after recovering at Letterman Army Hospital he was returned to Alcatraz; he is the only Alcatraz inmate known to have reached the shore by swimming, in worse conditions and with worse gear than Morris and the Anglins, which fed the theory that they could have made it too.

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / US Bureau of Prisons / Library of Congress — Carol M. Highsmith / Historic American Buildings Survey / US National Archives): John Paul Scott's Alcatraz mugshot (no. 1403); aerial view of Alcatraz; the cell house and guard tower; an Alcatraz menu (1946); Fort Point under the Golden Gate Bridge; the Golden Gate in November 1960
Archive film (public domain): 'US Army Special Forces Dive Team' (1956) — swimmers and rafts in open water; 'Golden Gate Bridge Opening' (1936) — illustrative, not Scott himself
Music: Satie, Gnossienne No. 1, public domain

post.facebook:
Officially, nobody ever escaped from Alcatraz. But one man swam all the way to the Golden Gate Bridge — and they found him alive.

In 29 years, 36 men tried to escape the Rock: six were shot dead, two drowned, five vanished in the freezing bay. In June 1962 three of them disappeared on a raft made of raincoats, and the guards said the bay had swallowed them.

Six months later, inmate 1403, John Paul Scott, set out to prove them wrong. On 16 December 1962 he slipped out of the cell house with a life jacket made of rubber kitchen gloves, blown up like balloons and tied to his arms. He jumped into the winter water and swam about 5 km through the currents everyone said nobody could survive — coming ashore at Fort Point, right under the Golden Gate Bridge. Teenagers found him on the rocks with hypothermia, too weak to run. He woke up in an army hospital and was sent straight back to Alcatraz.

He is the only prisoner known to have reached the shore by swimming — with worse gear than Frank Morris, in worse water. So if Scott made it… could Morris and the Anglins have made it too? 👇

youtube.description:
Officially, nobody ever escaped from Alcatraz. But one man swam all the way to the Golden Gate Bridge, and they found him alive.

Six months after Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers vanished in June 1962, Alcatraz inmate John Paul Scott tied inflated rubber gloves to his arms and swam about 5 km through the freezing San Francisco Bay to Fort Point, under the Golden Gate Bridge. Teenagers found him with hypothermia; he was sent back to Alcatraz. He is the only inmate known to have reached the shore by swimming — which raises the question: did Morris and the Anglins make it too?
